questionRef: 2024 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 2 A Q1
questionText: What was Antwerp’s population in the 1560s?

rows.verbatim: (About) 90,000 people

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract refers to Antwerp. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Antwerp was a city of about 90,000 people in the 1560s. Much of its business went to South Germany and Italy, inland by river and overland in wagons. It handled about a third of England’s cloth production.
To Spain it exported the candles for the great religious ceremonies. Also to Spain: corn, textiles, metals (copper, mercury and iron), as well as furs and amber.
Antwerp enjoyed a monopoly of spices such as pepper, ginger, cloves, cinnamon and mace, from the East, as well as sugar from the Canaries, Madeira and the Azores.

questionRef: 2024 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 3 A Q1
questionText: What advantage had Aragon over Castile?

rows.verbatim: It did not have to provide troops for military service beyond its borders

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract concerns Don Gaspar de Guzman, Count-Duke Olivares. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

The Count-Duke Olivares, first minister of Philip IV of Spain, considered that Castile bore too much responsibility, in peace and war, and the other Spanish kingdoms not enough. Aragon did not have to provide troops for military service beyond its own borders and Catalonia paid little in taxes. His attempts to extract more troops and money raised suspicion of Castilian domination and stout resistance, especially in Catalonia.
The assassination of Philip’s representative in Barcelona, in 1640, led to a full-scale Catalan revolt which it took the Spanish Crown twelve years to put down. The Portuguese, too, were in revolt. And there was a crisis in Spain’s Atlantic trade (no silver arrived in Seville in 1649).

questionRef: 2024 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 4 A Q1
questionText: Who went on the Grand Tour?

rows.verbatim: Young Englishmen/the sons of the aristocracy/tutors

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract concerns the Grand Tour. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

The Grand Tour was a leisurely journey through Europe, often lasting several years, by young Englishmen. In this way the sons of the aristocracy, often accompanied by a tutor, completed their education by enriching their knowledge of classical art and of European society.
The eventual destination was Italy, specifically Naples and Rome, where there were well- established colonies of English painters and architects.
As well as purchasing antique sculpture, those on the Tour bought present-day Italian paintings, including portraits of themselves, with which to adorn their houses.

questionRef: 2024 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 6 A Q1
questionText: Why were church lands to be sold?

rows.verbatim: To pay off public debts/to pay parish clergy

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract refers to church-state relations in Revolutionary France. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

On 2 November, 1789, it was decided that church lands were to be sold, to pay off public debt and to pay parish clergy.
The Civil Constitution of the Clergy was enacted in July, 1790. It provided for lay election of priests and bishops. Religious orders were to be dissolved except, for the time being, those engaged in educational and charity work. An oath of loyalty to the Constitution was to be imposed on all clergy.
The King, after some months’ delay, ratified the Civil Constitution, but the Pope rejected it. There would be ongoing tension between church and state in France.

questionRef: 2024 OL Early Modern Section Extra A Q1
questionText: Why did Henry VIII want a divorce in 1527?

rows.verbatim: He wanted to marry Anne Boleyn/he wanted a son

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
In this edited extract, historian Virginia Murphy outlines the background to the divorce of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

By the summer of 1527, Henry VIII had decided to divorce Catherine of Aragon, his wife of eighteen years, and marry Anne Boleyn. Earlier in 1527, the King revealed that he had developed doubts about the validity of his marriage because of Catherine’s previous marriage to his brother, Arthur.
Henry’s marriage with Catherine had produced only one surviving child, a girl, Mary. Was his lack of a son from the marriage God’s punishment for marrying his dead brother’s wife? The King needed a legitimate male heir to secure the Tudor dynasty.

questionRef: 2025 HL Later Modern Section 1 Q2(a)
questionText: To what extent do both documents question the value of marching on London? Explain your answer, referring to both documents.

rows.verbatim: Both documents question the value of marching on London, document A more so than document B. Points could include:
In doc A, the government view of marches on London is entirely negative. The statement says that such marches “can do no good”, are “liable to cause hardships” and are “altogether undesirable”.

The government states that the parliamentary system, where each voter has a member of parliament to represent him/her, is the only way to influence government policy, and that marches have no “constitutional role”.
The government sees marches as futile as no government minister will “consent” to meet any group of marchers.
Doc B also sees the shortcomings of marches, “these weary marches certainly are useless”. Doc B suggests that the purpose of some marches may be “propagandist” or to “stir up discontent”.

However, doc B also acknowledges the genuine grievances of the Jarrow marchers, “It is not to be wondered at that these men… should feel they have been neglected”. Marchers have been out of work for many months and whole towns have had “all their industries disappear”.
Doc B criticises parliament as often “forgetful, unimaginative and lazy”, and suggests that governments need to be prodded into action by “popular pressure”.

The writer praises the marchers for having drawn attention to the “desperate conditions” in Jarrow and sees the marchers not as troublemakers but as “men who are anxious that they shall not be forgotten”.

questionRef: 2025 HL Later Modern Section 1 Q2(b)
questionText: Which document more clearly depicts the social and economic problems of inter-war Britain? Explain your answer, referring to both documents.

rows.verbatim: Doc B more clearly depicts the social and economic problems of inter-war Britain.

Doc A contains no direct reference to the social and economic problems facing inter-war Britain. It criticises the holding of protest marches and defends the parliamentary system as the only method of conducting government business.

The statement carefully avoids naming the problems which have provoked the marches to take place, “In the opinion of His Majesty’s Government, such marches can do no good to the causes for which they are presented to be undertaken.” The “causes” are not named or addressed.
The government statement again evades identifying any problem in the dismissive phrase, “whatever their particular purpose” in the last paragraph.
In comparison, doc B refers directly to the “two hundred unemployed men” who are marching from Jarrow to London to present a petition to parliament.

The editorial refers to “men who have been out of work for many months” and to “whole towns which have seen all their industries disappear”. This reflects the social and economic problems affecting Britain at the time.
Doc B also refers to the sense of “neglect” felt by people in towns such as Jarrow and the anxiety of unemployed people “that they shall not be forgotten”.

questionRef: 2025 HL Later Modern Section 1 Q3(a)
questionText: From your knowledge of the Jarrow March, do you consider the points made by the government in document A convincing? Give reasons for your answer, referring to the document.

rows.verbatim: Yes and/or no, as to whether the points made in doc A are convincing.
rows.contextNote: Answers should refer to the doc and may also use relevant contextual knowledge.

rows.verbatim: The government statement makes a strong point as to how Britain is governed through parliamentary representation, rather than in response to public petitions and pressure. True to its word, the government did not meet with the Jarrow marchers when they arrived in London.

The government’s points are not convincing. The government had no effective response to offer to the Jarrow marchers, therefore they refused to meet them. The government was showing cowardice rather than the courage of its convictions in refusing to meet the marchers.

In this statement, the government refuses to even acknowledge why protestors are marching to London. The “causes” or “particular purpose” of the march are left unspecified, suggesting the government does not want to face up to the problems in towns such as Jarrow.

The government says that it follows normal procedures and is “always prepared to meet members of parliament”, but this is an insufficient/unconvincing response given the scale of the problems facing Jarrow in 1936.

The offhand response of the government, as shown in doc A, was proven by subsequent events in Jarrow, with the town only beginning to recover when the war caused demand for steel works and shipping to grow.

questionRef: 2025 HL Later Modern Section 1 Q3(b)
questionText: In what ways does document B illustrate the value of a newspaper editorial as historical source material? Make reference to the document in your answer.

rows.verbatim: The candidate may attempt to define what a newspaper editorial is: an opinion piece giving the editor’s point of view on an event in the news of the time. Unlike a newspaper report/article, an editorial does not give a full account of the event in question.
rows.contextNote: Candidates should assess the value of this newspaper editorial as a historical source on the Jarrow March.

rows.verbatim: It is of value because this is a primary source, written as the Jarrow March was in progress. A newspaper editor would usually have expert knowledge of current events and would be used to evaluating the circumstances and personalities relating to current events.
However, as editor of The Irish Times, this editor did not have first-hand experience of the march and was relying on reports made by other journalists to provide him with information on the march.

This editorial allows us to see how the Jarrow March was viewed at the time. The editor attempts to be even-handed in his treatment of the events in question. He seems to agree with the government that such marches “certainly are useless”, but he also thinks that the government statement takes “too narrow a view of the matter”, and that governments can be “unimaginative and lazy”.
He shows that there was public sympathy for the marchers at the time. He says the marchers’ aim was simply to make “a plea for work” and to draw attention to the “desperate conditions” in Jarrow.

This editorial lacks detailed factual information about the march. A historian should read newspaper reports as well as newspaper editorials to learn more about the key daily developments during the march.

questionRef: 2025 HL Early Modern Section 1 Q2(a)
questionText: Which document, A or B, expresses greater concern for the welfare of the kingdom? Explain your answer, referring to both documents.

rows.verbatim: Doc B expresses greater concern for the welfare of the kingdom
Doc A is the words of Henry VIII himself and mainly deals with concerns about his own family matters and his own qualms of conscience
He wonders about God’s will and fears that God is punishing him
In the third paragraph he says he fears for “the good of the kingdom” because he lacks a male heir
He says he is considering taking another wife for “the good of this noble realm”
It is as if he is justifying his divorce by saying it is for the good of the kingdom
The writer of Doc B criticises the impact of the divorce on England and describes its negative impact in detail
Cavendish mentions numerous “ill effects” including lies that have been told, the closure of “noble and ancient monasteries”, religious conflict, executions, and changes to the laws of England
He believes the kingdom has been almost destroyed and that the ill effects are ongoing, “the plague has not yet ceased”.

questionRef: 2025 HL Early Modern Section 1 Q2(b)
questionText: To what extent do both documents confirm the importance of the monarch at that time? Explain your answer, referring to both documents.

rows.verbatim: The importance of the monarch at that time could be reflected in points such as:

Marriages between European royal families are negotiated by diplomats who check the suitability and status of the prospective partners. These marriages are of high political and international importance.

Henry VIII has come to believe that God is indignant that he married his brother’s wife and therefore punished him by sending no male heirs. This reflects Henry’s inflated sense of his own importance.

Henry believes that the welfare of the kingdom is directly threatened by his lack of a male heir. He fears instability and danger if he does not have a son to succeed him. The welfare of the kingdom depends on the welfare of the king.

The fact that Cavendish did not write his account of the divorce until after Henry’s death suggests that the writer was too afraid of the king to write about the divorce during Henry’s life time. This shows the power and importance of Henry VIII, who dealt with his opponents by executing them.
Cavendish illustrates the importance of the monarchy by describing what he sees as the negative impact of Henry VIII on England.

Henry VIII’s “foolish” love life has brought ruination to the kingdom in many ways. Monasteries have been closed down, depriving the poor from the relief they used to provide. Religious conflicts and executions have caused the deaths of many people.
The “will and wilful desire” of the king has brought the noble kingdom almost to destruction.

The impact of a king’s actions far outlasts him, showing the king’s importance in society. The “fatal love” for Anne Boleyn was soon over but “the plague” caused by the king’s determination to divorce Catherine and marry Anne “has not yet ceased” even after several decades.

questionRef: 2025 HL Early Modern Section 1 Q3(a)
questionText: Do you find the king’s version of events in document A convincing? Explain your answer, making reference to the document and to your knowledge of the divorce of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon.

rows.verbatim: The king’s version of events can be seen as convincing and/or unconvincing.

The king speaks honestly of his doubts and troubles. He was worried by the words of the French ambassador, questioning his daughter’s legitimacy. His conscience is afflicted by a sense of guilt and he fears that God is punishing him. He considers the good of the kingdom as his primary focus rather than any dissatisfaction with his wife.

The king’s words are self-serving and hypocritical. He uses the words of the French ambassador, his alleged fear that God is punishing him and his apparent concern for the welfare of the kingdom as excuses to divorce the wife he no longer deems capable of producing a male heir.

The impact of Henry’s actions in declaring himself the head of the church, closing down and confiscating the wealth of the monasteries, executing those who opposed him (e.g. Thomas More) show that he was not concerned about the welfare of his kingdom but saw a way of increasing his own power and wealth.

questionRef: 2025 HL Early Modern Section 1 Q3(b)
questionText: Do you think that document B would have been published while Henry VIII was alive? Give reasons for your answer, making reference to the document.

rows.verbatim: No, the document would not have been published in Henry’s lifetime.

The document is highly critical of Henry VIII at a personal level, describing him as wilful/stubborn and stating that his obsession with Anne Boleyn was “foolish love”. He implies that Henry VIII was fickle, “the fatal love lasted but a short time”.

The document is also highly critical of the impact of Henry VIII’s actions on England, describing the destruction of the monasteries, religious conflict and executions that have taken place due to Henry VIII. He accuses the king of almost destroying the kingdom, which would have been seen as treason during Henry’s lifetime.

Henry did not tolerate criticism or opposition to his wishes. He executed two of his wives, and important courtiers such as Thomas More and Thomas Cromwell, etc. Cavendish would not have dared to publish such an account as is given in Doc B in Henry’s lifetime.

questionRef: 2025 OL Later Modern Section 2 Topic 2 A Q1
questionText: Where was Parnell arrested?

rows.verbatim: Morrison’s Hotel, Dawson Street, Dublin
rows.contextNote: (one element only = 3m)

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This is an edited extract from a newspaper account of Parnell’s arrest, 13 October, 1881. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

On Thursday morning, 13 October, 1881, Parnell was arrested at Morrison’s Hotel, Dawson Street, Dublin. He was lodged in Kilmainham prison before the citizens of Dublin were fully awake.
There was no disturbance in the streets for no one knew why the four-wheeled cabs waited so long before the hotel. It was not until some police constables added themselves to the procession that suspicions arose.
Parnell himself swore the servants of the hotel to secrecy as if he knew that the arrest was coming.

questionRef: 2025 OL Later Modern Section 2 Topic 3 A Q1
questionText: When was the economist’s report compiled?

rows.verbatim: December 1940

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract refers to Northern Ireland’s war effort during World War II. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

In December 1940 an economist compiled a report on Northern Ireland’s contribution to the war effort for the War Cabinet in London.
He concluded that, to date, its role had been negligible, although it had suffered less from enemy action than any other part of the United Kingdom. Since 1939, he noted, the siren [warning of an air raid] had sounded only five times in Belfast, and each time it was a false alarm, in marked and deadly contrast to other British cities.
That was changed by the massive German air raids on Belfast on the nights of 15-16 April and 4-5 May, 1941.

questionRef: 2025 OL Later Modern Section 2 Topic 4 A Q1
questionText: From where did de Valera escape?

rows.verbatim: From Lincoln Jail

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
After his escape from Lincoln Jail in February, 1919, Éamon de Valera announced his decision to go to America to seek support for the Irish cause. This edited extract reveals the reaction of IRA Volunteers to his decision. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

We felt de Valera’s departure would be a fatal mistake, that the country would misunderstand his motives and regard it as selfish, or even cowardly desertion.
When this view was expressed, Collins replied: ‘I told him so, but you know what it is to try to argue with Dev. He feels the place where he can be useful is America.’
The Volunteers took the view that the place for an Irish leader was in Ireland.

questionRef: 2025 OL Later Modern Section 2 Topic 5 A Q1
questionText: What was introduced on 5 July, 1948?

rows.verbatim: The National Health Service (NHS)

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
In this edited extract historian Marianne Elliott, who grew up in Belfast, notes the impact of the National Health Service (NHS). Read it and answer the questions which follow.

The National Health Service was introduced on 5 July, 1948. It transformed the lives of families such as ours. Suddenly, everything we could not afford before was free.
There was a rush for dental treatment and spectacles and there was over-prescription of the now-free drugs.
Unfortunately, the health legislation did not permit hospitals with religious links to maintain their ethos within the health service. So the Catholic-run Mater Hospital, Belfast, was excluded from state funding.

questionRef: 2025 OL Later Modern Section 2 Topic 6 A Q1
questionText: Why did the Irish attempt to join the EEC fail in January 1961?

rows.verbatim: De Gaulle rejected the application

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
In this edited extract, Garret FitzGerald reflects on the impact of the EEC on Irish fisheries. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

The Irish application to join the EEC was turned down by General de Gaulle, with that of Britain, in January 1961.
By the time Ireland, Britain and Denmark joined in 1973, the original six members had brought about an arrangement that gave them access to British, Danish and Irish fish stocks.
The disadvantages of this arrangement for Ireland were lessened by a deal that I secured, as Foreign Minister, in 1976. This enabled Ireland to double its fish catches and increase their value by 40% within a few years.

questionRef: 2025 OL Later Modern Section 3 Topic 1 A Q1
questionText: What was one form of entertainment provided by the Emperor?

rows.verbatim: Balls/banquets/theatrical entertainments

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract deals with the difficulties faced by Emperor Francis II of Austria during the Congress of Vienna, 1815. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

During the Congress Emperor Francis had to entertain many royal visitors with balls, banquets and theatrical entertainments.
Every night dinner at his palace was laid at forty tables. Special liveries and carriages were provided for all his guests. The horses in the stable numbered no less than 1,400.
Each monarch had brought with him a crowd of followers and the royal wives were attended by ladies-in-waiting. Francis was driven to distraction by providing amusement for them and by problems of precedence.

questionRef: 2025 OL Later Modern Section 3 Topic 2 A Q1
questionText: What was introduced on 2 March, 1916?

rows.verbatim: Conscription [for men]

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract deals with women in the workforce in Britain during World War I. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Even before World War I women were moving into commerce and the professions. By 1914 a quarter of all clerks were women.
After the beginning of conscription for men on 2 March, 1916, the government began an active drive to fill the places of the men with female labour. Over a million women, for the first time, embarked on paid work. They drove trams, worked on the land, took on munitions work and nursed the sick.
In this way working-class women escaped from the drudgery of domestic service. Middle- class women escaped stifling pre-war conventions. They became more aware of employment opportunities and now had their own income.

questionRef: 2025 OL Later Modern Section 3 Topic 4 A Q1
questionText: What was attempted by the Second Vatican Council?

rows.verbatim: To adapt the Catholic church to a changing world

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract deals with the Second Vatican Council (1962-1965). Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Assembled by Pope John XXIII, the Second Vatican Council was held in Rome in 1962-1965 and attempted to adapt the Catholic Church to a changing world.
It abolished the compulsory use of Latin for church services which could now be carried on in the language of the worshippers.
It aimed to eliminate anti-Semitism and to establish better relations with other churches.
The Pope and his successor, Pope Paul VI, abandoned the papal triple crown and complex styles of dress in an attempt to engage with the modern world.

questionRef: 2025 OL Later Modern Section 3 Topic 6 A Q1
questionText: How were space launches carried out a decade before?

rows.verbatim: They were carried out in secret/high security

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
In this edited extract, journalist Edwin Diamond comments on the media coverage of the Apollo 11 mission. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Less than a decade ago space launchings were secret events held behind high security barriers. Not so today when, at Cape Kennedy, a media city springs up for each launching.
For Apollo 11 there were 4,000 reporters. A trailer city of radio and TV vans brought the event live to a world-wide audience.
After the launching, much of the news corps was flown to Houston, Texas, where NASA kept them informed of developments twenty-four hours a day.

questionRef: 2025 OL Early Modern Section 2 Topic 2 A Q1
questionText: Who was Grace O’Malley’s first husband?

rows.verbatim: Donal O’Flaherty

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
In this edited extract, historian Hiram Morgan writes about Grace O’Malley. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Grace O’Malley married first Donal O’Flaherty and later Richard Bourke. She was powerful in her own right due to the considerable naval power of the O’Malleys.
Despite clashes with the Crown, which imprisoned her in 1577-1579, she urged her menfolk to seek agreement with the Tudor state.
While in London in 1593, she petitioned Queen Elizabeth I for a grant of lands because, under Gaelic law, she was not entitled, as a widow, to any part of her husband’s estate.

questionRef: 2025 OL Early Modern Section 2 Topic 3 A Q1
questionText: From where did Keating return to Ireland?

rows.verbatim: Bordeaux/France

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract is from an article by historian Bernadette Cunningham on Geoffrey Keating’s Foras Feasa. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Geoffrey Keating was associated with the Irish college in Bordeaux, probably as a teacher, before returning to Ireland, as a priest, about 1610.
It is for his narrative history of Ireland ‘Foras Feasa ar Éirinn’ [‘Compendium of Wisdom about Ireland’] that Keating is best known. It told the story of Ireland from the creation of the world down to the coming of the Normans in the 12th century.
It circulated in manuscript [hand-written] form and was first published in printed form in 1723.
It criticised the unfavourable views of Ireland published by earlier writers. Keating excluded from his definition of Irish people those who were not born in Ireland and those who were not Catholics.

questionRef: 2025 OL Early Modern Section 2 Topic 4 A Q1
questionText: What did the Cattle Acts of 1663 and 1667 ban?

rows.verbatim: Banned the import of live Irish cattle to England

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract deals with trade restrictions and how they affected Ireland. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

The Cattle Acts of 1663 and 1667 banned the import of live Irish cattle to England. The Staple Act of 1663 required that certain items from the colonies could not be landed directly in Ireland but had to be shipped to England and re-exported to Ireland.
The main effect of this was to increase the cost of colonial imports into Ireland, in the case of tobacco by 8%. The result was a considerable rise in smuggling. However, the impact was less than expected due to a shift from the export of raw materials to processed goods with a higher value added.

questionRef: 2025 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 3 A Q1
questionText: What did Puritans attempt to promote?

rows.verbatim: Godliness and virtue

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract notes Puritan attempts to promote ‘godliness and virtue’ in the England of Oliver Cromwell. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Religious practice on the Sabbath Day [Sunday] was enforced.
Anti-gambling laws were introduced, ale houses were closed and, for a time, theatres. Race meetings were banned, as well as cockfights and duels.
‘Rowdy’ and ‘superstitious’ practices became illegal, like dancing around the maypole or celebrating Christmas.

questionRef: 2025 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 4 A Q1
questionText: What did de Vauban produce in 1669?

rows.verbatim: A treatise on siege-warfare

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract refers to Sébastien le Prestre de Vauban. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

De Vauban was Louis XIV’s main military engineer. He was commissioned in the French army in 1655. In 1669, he compiled an influential treatise on siege-warfare.
Over the period 1672-1678 he carried out nearly twenty successful sieges. He used a succession of parallel trenches to give advancing troops protection. His fortifications took advantage of local geography to enable defenders to pour a cross-fire into attackers. He developed the use of the bayonet, first used at Bayonne in 1650.
In spite of enjoying royal favour for most of his career, he died in disgrace, after writing a pamphlet on taxation of which Louis XIV disapproved.

questionRef: 2025 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 5 A Q1
questionText: What did the Tea Act seek to do?

rows.verbatim: To relieve the financial stresses of the East India Company/let the East India company export/sell tea to the American colonies

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract refers to the Boston Tea Party. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

The Tea Act, 1773, was an attempt to relieve the financial stresses of the East India Company by permitting it to export tea to the American colonies directly and to sell it there.
It would make tea cheaper for the consumer. But it threatened the interests of both colonial merchants and smuggling rings, so those two powerful groups opposed it.
In Boston, on 16 December, 1773, a body of men, disguised as Indians, and directed by Sam Adams, boarded the tea-ships and threw their cargoes into the harbour.

questionRef: 2025 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 6 A Q1
questionText: What and where was the Bastille?

rows.verbatim: A prison
in Paris

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
In this edited extract, historian Simon Schama notes conditions, for better-off prisoners, in the Bastille prison, Paris. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

No one wanted to be in the Bastille. But, once there, life – for the more privileged – could be made bearable.
Alcohol and tobacco were allowed and, under King Louis XVI, card games were introduced for anyone sharing a cell. Also, a billiard table was allowed for the Breton gentry who requested one.
Some of the literary inmates even thought that a spell in the Bastille would make them famous as champions of liberty. The Abbé Morellet, for example, wrote: ‘I would be better known and make my fortune.’

questionText: Where had Alonso Morales recently arrived?

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract gives the views of Alonso Morales, recently arrived in the New World. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Alonso Morales, still under twenty, has recently arrived in the New World. He came in the company of his cousin who paid his fare from Spain. Alonso is now working to pay off the debt as a tailor in his cousin’s shop.
Food is cheap and plentiful, he claims. Every Spaniard has a horse. There is plenty of work and workers are paid very well. Goods from Spain are scarce and expensive, however.

questionRef: 2026 HL Later Modern Section 1 Q2(a)
questionText: What contrasting views of hurlers and hurling are offered in the documents? Refer to both documents in your answer.

rows.verbatim: Doc A gives a very negative account of the hurlers/hurling, whereas doc B offers a much more positive account. Points could include:

In doc A, the writer is filled with dismay at the sight of “idle, pale, emaciated” locals and their apparent laziness. He sees this as proof that GAA officers have not been carrying out their duties and getting people out to practise hurling.
There are no spectators at the hurling match, showing that the GAA is not attracting loyal support in Kilkenny.
He says the hurling is the “worst” he has ever seen and that members of the teams lay down to rest even as the contest continued.
Others sneaked off to go drinking instead of staying at the match.
Doc B shows that the GAA had a strong presence in Charleville, with members of half a dozen local clubs present for the Archbishop’s visit.
Members of the GAA were dressed in club uniforms, marched in disciplined formations and carried out the commands of their captains.
The Archbishop is impressed that GAA members do not fight with each other, do not drink to excess and are always present at Sunday Mass.
The hurlers parade in front of the Archbishop’s carriage, contributing to the air of festivity and rejoicing in the town.

questionRef: 2026 HL Later Modern Section 1 Q2(b)
questionText: To what extent do both documents suggest that the writers were concerned about matters other than sport? Refer to both documents in your answer.

rows.verbatim: The writers of both documents are concerned about matters other than sport.
The writer of doc A gives evidence of social problems he witnessed in Kilkenny, whereas doc B refers to problems which are not to be found among members of the GAA in Charleville.

Doc A: the writer comments on the pale, poorly nourished appearance of local people and on their listless attitude. People are “idle” and lazy. The hurlers lack energy, stopping to rest during the game. The writer is also concerned that people are sneaking off to go drinking.

Doc B: the writer reports the Archbishops’ concerns about the dangers of bad blood/fighting, drink and the neglect of religious duties. However, his fears have proved groundless, for the most part. The writer gives a very favourable description of the discipline and energy of the GAA members and the positive atmosphere in Charleville.

rows.contextNote: Candidates should refer to the doc in their answers — A clear understanding of the meaning of “objective” is necessary to gain marks in the very good to excellent range.

rows.verbatim: Doc A is written by Michael Cusack, a founder of the GAA, who therefore has a particular point of view on the importance of the GAA and how it is developing. Cusack’s sense of dismay and disapproval comes across very strongly, showing that this account is emotional rather than objective.

It could be argued that even though he is the founder of the GAA, Cusack does not try to gloss over the faults he sees, and reports on the poor attitude of the people to the GAA, the low standard of hurling, etc.
The report is objective in that it offers definite factual information about named places in Kilkenny, the numbers involved in the hurling match, etc.

questionRef: 2026 HL Later Modern Section 1 Q3(b)
questionText: In what ways is document B a useful source for the historian investigating the history of the GAA? Refer to the document in your answer.

rows.verbatim: Doc B is a useful historical source on the early history of the GAA.
rows.contextNote: Points should be supported by reference to doc B.

rows.verbatim: The account was written in 1887, just three years after the founding of the GAA, and offers useful evidence on how the GAA was developing in north Cork.
It shows the sense of pride and discipline among members of the GAA, and suggests the power of the GAA went beyond sporting matters.
It quotes the views of an important early patron of the GAA, Archbishop Croke.
It gives an insight into possible social problems in Ireland at the time, such as “bad blood” and drinking to excess.
It suggests the power of the Catholic Church in Ireland in the late 19th century. The Archbishop’s visit to Charleville is a cause of festivity and rejoicing, etc.

questionRef: 2026 HL Early Modern Section 1 Q2(b)
questionText: Do the documents agree on how the leaders of Gaelic Ireland should be treated? Give reasons for your answer, referring to the documents.

rows.verbatim: There are similarities in how the documents advise dealing with the leaders of Gaelic Ireland, but there are some differences also.
rows.contextNote: Points should be supported by reference to both documents, e.g.,

rows.verbatim: In doc A, the writer recommends a policy of “mercy” and “force” which would see “some” Irish chiefs rewarded with titles of honour such as earl, baron or knight. This would help to transform them into civil, humble, well-governed Christians. The document does not say what should happen to those who cannot be brought to “quiet obedience and order”.

In Doc B, the writer would like to bring the wild Irish under control by “force of arms” and take their lands from them and banish them. However, due to war with France and lack of funds, the English authorities cannot follow this “right” course of action and must instead do what is “expedient”. They must reach a settlement with the O’Mores and O’Connors of Laois and Offaly “at any cost”. This will mean pardoning the chiefs and giving them back some of their lands.

questionRef: 2026 HL Early Modern Section 1 Q3(a)
questionText: Would you consider document A to be an objective source? Give reasons for your answer, referring to the document.

rows.verbatim: Doc A is written from an English point-of-view and is not objective in its description of the Irish who are described in highly pejorative terms. The Gaelic Irish “live like beasts”. He claims they have no knowledge of God, or good manners and no way of dealing with crimes such as murder and robbery. At least some of this is factually incorrect. The Irish Church was well developed with monasteries established in all parts of the country. A system of justice was in operation in Ireland, the Brehon law system. Neither was it true to say that the Irish did not farm.
rows.contextNote: Candidates should refer to the doc in their answers. — A clear understanding of the meaning of “objective” is necessary to gain marks in the very good to excellent range.

rows.verbatim: This document is not written to provide a factual description of Ireland but to justify bringing the Irish “to quiet obedience and order” through the use of “substantial garrisons” and “force”.

The writer sees the English as the proper rulers of Ireland who can bestow “mercy” on the subdued Irish, and transform them from rude, beastly, ignorant and unruly infidels to civil, reasonable, humble and well-governed Christians.

questionRef: 2026 HL Early Modern Section 1 Q3(b)
questionText: In what ways is document B a useful source for the historian investigating the Plantation of Laois‐Offaly? Make reference to the document in your answer.

rows.verbatim: Doc B is a useful historical source on the Laois Offaly Plantation.
rows.contextNote: Comments on the limitations of the document should also be accepted. — Points should be supported by reference to doc B.

rows.verbatim: The account was written in 1558, and is a primary source of evidence on the background to the Plantation.

The writer is supportive of British rule in Ireland and gives a very hostile account of the “wild Irish”. Although it is a biased account, this document provides evidence of how the English viewed the “barbarous” Irish.

The document provides evidence of a sense of crisis for English rule in Ireland at the time. English power is threatened with “extinction”, the small army and lack of funds mean that war against the Irish is “futile”. A settlement must be reached “at any cost”.
The document shows English policy in Ireland was determined by expedience rather that by “what is right”.
Factual details such as the size of the English army in Ireland and the potential rental income from the lands of Laois and Offaly are useful information for historians, etc.

Treaty published in all the papers this morning. President de Valera in an awful state.

questionRef: 2026 OL Later Modern Section 2 Topic 4 A Q1
questionText: What two groups came to dominate Five Points?

rows.verbatim: Irish Catholic immigrants and African-Americans

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract deals with the Five Points district, a poor quarter of New York. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

The two poorest groups of New Yorkers – Irish Catholic immigrants and African‐Americans – quickly came to dominate Five Points. The neighbourhood’s raucous saloons and dancehalls made it notorious. So, too, did the drunken brawls that the two groups engaged in.
However, its drunks and crooks were outnumbered by hardworking, law‐abiding immigrants, who saved money to support aged parents back in Ireland and to bring more of their countrymen to America. They also sought to protect themselves against the contagious diseases, such as cholera and measles, that spread like wildfire.

questionText: What problem was expected to arise in Derry?

rows.verbatim: Problems linked to the activities of the ABOD/widespread discord and bloodshed

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract, from a report prepared for the Dublin government, anticipated problems linked to the activities of Apprentice Boys in Derry in August 1969. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

questionRef: 2026 OL Later Modern Section 2 Topic 6 A Q1
questionText: Who celebrated the 10 o’clock Mass?

rows.verbatim: Bishop James Fergus

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
In this edited extract journalist Patsy McGarry recalls the impact of Vatican II. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

The second Vatican Council had begun in 1962. Every Sunday when he was back in Ballaghaderreen from Rome, Bishop James Fergus would celebrate the Children’s Mass at 10 o’clock.
He would tell us about what was happening at the Council and the changes it might bring. I was excited by the opening of the Catholic Church to the world and by the promise of greater social justice.
I saw the gloom of the Cathedral eliminated by bright colours, with the priest facing us at Mass and speaking in English or Irish, instead of Latin.

questionRef: 2026 OL Later Modern Section 3 Topic 1 A Q1
questionText: What position was held by Baron Haussmann?

rows.verbatim: Prefect of the Seine

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract refers to Haussmann’s Paris. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

The most famous project of urban renewal was begun by Baron Haussmann soon after his appointment as Prefect of the Seine in 1853. His aim was to rid Paris of its ancient narrow streets and replace them with broad boulevards. This would remove what had been ideal sites for the construction of barricades by revolutionary crowds and open the city to the forces of order.
His grand schemes reduced the Île de la Cité’s population from 15,000 to 5,000, devastating nearly all the private dwellings there at one stroke. ‘It was the gutting of Old Paris,’ he boasted in his memoirs. Now the way was open for the construction of grand public buildings, such as the Opéra and the creation of the major railway stations.

rows.verbatim: Germany is now powerful/prosperous

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:

questionText: How had transport improved?

rows.verbatim: Broad avenues for cars/new metro stations

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.

This edited extract describes Moscow in the 1930s. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Moscow was transformed in a few years from a rundown city of churches into an imperial capital with apartment blocks, department stores, places of culture, parks and sporting arenas.
Streets were cleared to build broad avenues for cars that rolled off the production lines. The metro stations were like cathedrals, with spacious halls, marble floors, chandeliers and depictions of the achievements of the Five Year Plans.
All of this stood in stark contrast to the people’s squalid living conditions in apartments where several families shared a few divided rooms and a kitchen.

questionRef: 2026 OL Later Modern Section 3 Topic 4 A Q1
questionText: When did the Soviet army arrive in Budapest?

rows.verbatim: 4th November

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
On the morning of 4 November 1956, the Soviet army invaded Budapest, Hungary. This edited extract notes what a journalist could see and hear from the windows of a newspaper building.

At the moment there is silence. It may be the silence before the storm. We have no heavy weapons, only light machine‐guns and rifles.
People are jumping up at the tanks, throwing hand grenades and then slamming the drivers’ windows. The Hungarian people are not afraid of death. It is only a pity that they cannot resist for long.
The Soviet tanks are getting nearer and there is heavy artillery. What is the United Nations doing? Give us a little encouragement.

In this edited extract, Harold Macmillan, then UK Chancellor of the Exchequer, recalls a meeting with a US delegation that took place in London a couple of days after Egypt’s Gamal Abdul Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

I met the Americans at 6.30. We had an hour’s talk. I told them as plainly as I could, that we must get Nasser out, either by diplomacy or war. It was a question not only of honour but of survival for us.
I think they were quite alarmed for they had hoped to find me less extreme. If we keep the Americans really frightened, they will help us get what we want – international control of the Suez Canal and the collapse of Nasser.

questionRef: 2026 OL Later Modern Section 3 Topic 6 A Q1
questionText: What did Billy Graham want preserved?

rows.verbatim: The American way of life

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This is an edited extract from a letter from the religious leader Billy Graham to President Eisenhower (2 December 1957). Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Sacrifice and renewed dedication will be needed if the American way of life is to be preserved. We Americans are growing soft. Our amusements and greed for money are acting as a sedative.
We almost need compulsory scientific training in all our schools, as well as compulsory physical training for all our young people.
The American people need to be encouraged to look to God who is the source of all our spiritual and moral strength.

questionRef: 2026 OL Later Modern Section Extra A Q1
questionText: When and where did the meeting take place?

rows.verbatim: Westminster Palace Hotel and March 1886

notes: Later Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
In this edited extract, Parnell announces Gladstone’s acceptance of Home Rule. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

In March, 1886, when we were on the eve of the Home Rule Bill, Parnell summoned a few of us to the Westminster Palace Hotel, London, to hear the result of his conversation with Gladstone.
We met on a raw, foggy night with our hearts on fire. The thought that a British Prime Minister had agreed to our dream quickened our pulses.
As Parnell revealed details, however, we grew disheartened at the meanness of Gladstone’s offer, especially as regards finance. Towards midnight, disappointed, we went out into the fog and frost.

questionRef: 2026 OL Early Modern Section 2 Topic 2 A Q1
questionText: Which church did Meiler Magrath leave?

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
In this edited extract historian Richard Bagwell (1840‐1918) criticises Meiler Magrath. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Meiler Magrath was no credit either to the Catholic Church which he deserted or the Protestant Church which he joined. In 1607 he had been Archbishop of Cashel and Bishop of Emly for thirty‐six years. Both dioceses were found to be in a terrible state.

questionRef: 2026 OL Early Modern Section 2 Topic 3 A Q1
questionText: When did Elizabeth Butler become Countess of Ormond?
notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract refers to Elizabeth Butler, Countess of Ormond. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

In 1633, Elizabeth Butler became the Countess of Ormond on her husband’s succession to the earldom. On the outbreak of the 1641 rebellion she moved to Kilkenny Castle, the family seat [residence].
When the city became the capital of the Catholic Confederation she assisted Protestant refugees, giving them shelter in the Castle.
In 1647, she followed her husband to England on his surrender of Dublin to parliamentary forces. When he decided to renew his fight for the Royalist cause she departed for France.

questionRef: 2026 OL Early Modern Section 2 Topic 4 A Q1
questionText: What were rapparees?

rows.verbatim: Outlaws/bandits

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
Rapparees were outlaws and bandits who robbed houses and travellers or extorted protection money. This edited extract, from their time, describes how they operated. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

When the rapparees do not wish to show their faces on the bogs they sink down into long grass, so that it would be as easy to find a hare as one of them.
They hide their weapons in this way: they take the lock off their musket and put it in their pocket or hide it in some dry place; they close the muzzle with a cork and the touch‐hole with a small feather; they throw the weapon itself into running water or a pond.
But, when they want to do mischief, they can be ready in an hour. Everyone knows where to find his weapon, though you do not.

This edited extract, from a letter dated 27 March 1772, describes an attack by Steel Boys on a “big house” in Co. Wexford. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Last night 200 of them came to my Uncle Daniel’s about 12 o’clock. They set fire to his barn and stable, a hay stack and a quantity of straw in another stack.
They took shelter and fired constantly at the house. Its defenders, although they fired out, could not get a clean shot at them.
Further loss consists of a large quantity of oats, some wheat, and timber which had been stored in the stable.
Almost all of their fodder is gone. All their windows were broken. But the horses were saved.

questionRef: 2026 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 1 A Q1
questionText: What was one way in which the couple should arrive at church?

rows.verbatim: They should arrive on time/without musicians

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract refers to Calvin’s Geneva. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

When the time comes for the marriage service the parties should arrive at church without drummers or fiddlers. They shall present themselves in a way proper to Christians, before the church bell rings, so that the marriage can be blessed before the sermon. If they are late or negligent, then they should be sent away.
Also, during married life, when children arrive, the use of the names of the patron saints is forbidden. That would be an encouragement to superstition and idolatry. The names of kings are forbidden too.

questionText: What did the Jesuit Fathers fear?

rows.verbatim: They feared causing suspicion among the Chinese

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
In this edited extract Matteo Ricci writes about the beginning of the Jesuit mission in China.

For fear the new religion might cause suspicion among the Chinese, the Fathers did not speak openly about religious matters when they first appeared in public.
As well as receiving visitors, they spent time studying the Chinese language, the methods of writing and the customs of the people.
They hoped to impress the Chinese by example and by the sanctity [holiness] of their lives.
They wore the ordinary Chinese outer garment, which was somewhat similar to their own religious habits: a long robe reaching down to the heels and very wide sleeves.

questionRef: 2026 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 3 A Q1
questionText: What was one key feature of the climate change mentioned?

rows.verbatim: It was a period of severe cooling/temperatures dropped by 2°C

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract refers to climate change. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Environmental historians now recognise the seventeenth century as a period of intense climate change, the peak of the Little Ice Age – a period of severe cooling in which average yearly temperatures, in the northern hemisphere, plunged by as much as two degrees Celsius.
Crop failure led to food shortages. An unusual rate of volcanic activity hurled enough sulphur dioxide into the upper stratosphere to dim the sun for decades, contributing to already low temperatures and stunting crops.
All of which led to a search for people to blame. In southern Germany in 1626 a spring hailstorm, followed by sudden Arctic temperatures, prompted the torture and execution of 900 men and women, accused of creating the storm by witchcraft.

questionRef: 2026 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 4 A Q1
questionText: What was one feature of the architecture of Moscow?

rows.verbatim: Wooden buildings/narrow streets

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract refers to early eighteenth‐century Moscow. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

Moscow was a dangerous and violent place. The town consisted almost entirely of wooden buildings. Clustered together in narrow streets, they were the subject of devastating fires.
In the summer of 1706 the English Ambassador had to flee his house as fire took hold. “God be thanked my house still stands,” he wrote, “but all the street around me is burnt down!”
Moscow was notorious for its beggars and thieves. It was an expensive place in which to live. “My pocket is empty,” the Ambassador complained. He soon came to realise that nothing could be achieved without generous bribes and presents to the Russian ministers.

questionRef: 2026 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 5 A Q1
questionText: Who attacked the East India Company’s settlement in Calcutta?

rows.verbatim: The Nawab of Bengal

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract refers to Robert Clive. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

In 1756 the Nawab of Bengal attacked the English East India Company’s settlement at Calcutta. His treatment of his English prisoners, many of whom suffocated in the soon legendary “Black Hole of Calcutta”, gave additional offence.
The East India Company’s army, commanded by its employee, Robert Clive, took the city and then, on 22 June 1757, won a battle over the Nawab’s much larger forces at Plassey, about 100 miles from Calcutta.
Clive emerged as Governor and Commander‐in‐Chief of Bengal, by which time the Mughal Emperor had granted the East India Company responsibility for the administration of the area, including the right to collect taxes.

questionRef: 2026 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 5 A Q2
questionText: What happened in the “Black Hole of Calcutta”?

rows.verbatim: English prisoners suffocated

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract refers to Robert Clive. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

In 1756 the Nawab of Bengal attacked the English East India Company’s settlement at Calcutta. His treatment of his English prisoners, many of whom suffocated in the soon legendary “Black Hole of Calcutta”, gave additional offence.
The East India Company’s army, commanded by its employee, Robert Clive, took the city and then, on 22 June 1757, won a battle over the Nawab’s much larger forces at Plassey, about 100 miles from Calcutta.
Clive emerged as Governor and Commander‐in‐Chief of Bengal, by which time the Mughal Emperor had granted the East India Company responsibility for the administration of the area, including the right to collect taxes.

questionRef: 2026 OL Early Modern Section 3 Topic 6 A Q1
questionText: Why was the Revolutionary Tribunal set up?

rows.verbatim: To deal with enemies of the revolution

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract notes an aspect of the French Reign of Terror. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

In the capital sat the highest court of revolutionary France, the Revolutionary Tribunal of Paris, which had been established in the spring of 1793 to deal with enemies of the revolution. Its activities were stepped up in October, 1793, when the desire for vengeance against traitors to the republic seems to have reached its peak.
Among the most prominent victims at this time were the Queen, Marie Antoinette, and several former generals who had not shown sufficient enthusiasm for the new regime. All met their death on the guillotine which stood on the Place de la Revolution.
The Revolutionary Tribunal was responsible for 2,639 victims. Estimates of the total number of victims under the Reign of Terror reach 20,000.

questionRef: 2026 OL Early Modern Section Extra A Q1
questionText: Who employed the poet?

rows.verbatim: A patron/local chieftain

notes: Early Modern field of study. The scheme prints '6M' for this ask.
stem:
This edited extract refers to bardic schools and to those who were trained in them. Read it and answer the questions which follow.

The file [“poet” or “bard”], the product of the bardic schools, was employed by a patron, the local chieftain, to praise him and his family, to note his famous ancestors, and to mourn his death.
The filí were an extremely influential group in society and it was they who set the written standard of Irish. Poetry was a profession, usually handed down from father to son. It required a special training in language, which was provided by bardic schools.
